newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian Moslem scholar writes rejoinder to Rushdie.
newsitem.headline: Indian Moslem scholar writes rejoinder to Rushdie.

text.p: A Moslem scholar said on Thursday he has written a "blow-by-blow" rejoinder to Salman Rushdie's novel "The Satanic Verses" which he said could increase the danger to the British author's life.

Hafiz Zahir Uddin Qadri, a Moslem imam (cleric) in the northern Indian town of Kanpur, told Reuters his 1,200-page book was being translated from Urdu into English and will be titled "The Final Verses".
"I was provoked to write this book after I read the nonsense published by Rushdie during my visit to England in 1990," Qadri told Reuters in a telephone interview.
Qadri acknowledged that his work, which has already been published in Urdu, could reinforce Moslems' anger against Rushdie.
"Therefore I would not be surprised if the danger to Rushdie's life escalates after the publication of my book in English."
The Asian Age newspaper said in a front-page story on Thursday that the English version was set for release in March.
In 1989 an Iranian foundation offered a $2 million reward for the killing of Rushdie.

The 15th Khordad Foundation offered the reward after Iran's late leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini issued a fatwa, or religious edict, imposing the death sentence on Rushdie for alleged blasphemy against Islam in "The Satanic Verses".
Since the edict was issued, Rushdie has been under 24-hour police protection, although he has in the past year been appearing more often in public.
On Wednesday an Iranian newspaper said the foundation had raised the reward to $2.5 million.
Iranian officials say the death threat is a purely religious matter, unrelated to the government. Tehran has said it would not pursue Rushdie but also stresses it cannot withdraw a religious edict.
Qadri said he wrote his book, currently being translated at the Jamia Millia University in Delhi, to prevent young Moslems from being "misled" by Rushdie's writings.
